1296.title: The option for the poor
1296.hook: a rich man passes a poor man at his gate every day, and never once sees him
1296.howItsDone: Catholics live this through parish food pantries, the Society of St. Vincent de Paul, Catholic Charities and similar works, and through advocacy that asks how laws and budgets affect the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cain's dodge, and the answer: yes. Your line was rights and duties.

A rich man's gate. He goes in and out in purple and fine linen, and feasts every day. At the same gate lies a poor man covered in sores, wishing for the crumbs that fall from the table. Jesus tells this story in Luke, and two details stand out. The poor man has a name, Lazarus; the rich man never gets one. And the rich man is never cruel. He doesn't kick Lazarus or send him away. He simply does nothing for him, day after day. Catholic social teaching has a phrase meant to make that kind of passing by hard. Today, the preferential option for the poor.
screen: `A RICH MAN'S GATE.` → `THE POOR MAN HAS A NAME.` → `THE RICH MAN DOES NOTHING.`

segments.voice: First, what preferential means here. It doesn't mean God loves poor people more and everyone else less. At a family table, if one child is sick, that child gets served first, and nobody thinks the others are loved less. The Catechism speaks of the Church's preferential love for those oppressed by poverty in that sense: the ones in greatest need get attention first. Second, where it comes from. In Luke, Jesus opens his teaching on the plain like this, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are ye poor, for yours is the kingdom of God." The Greek word there is ptochos, a word for the poor who depend on others to live. Not a footnote to the gospel: the first blessing in that sermon. Third, what it isn't. It isn't meant to set one class against another, and it isn't a task for the poor alone. It's asked of every Christian, rich and poor alike. John Paul the Second called it a special form of primacy in the exercise of Christian charity. Fourth, how it works. The phrase gives a lens for judging any decision, from a nation's budget to a parish schedule to a household's spending: how does this land on the people with the least? Who is lying at this particular gate? Back in the story, the rich man's failure wasn't one cruel choice against Lazarus. It was ordinary choices, day after day, made as if Lazarus weren't there.
screen: `SERVED FIRST, NOT LOVED MORE.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE YE POOR.` · `NOT AGAINST ANYONE.` · then: `A LENS FOR EVERY DECISION.`

segments.voice: Pick a decision in front of you this week: where to shop, how to vote on something, a rule at work, what to do with a little extra money. Then walk around to the other side of the gate and ask who in your town has the least, and how this lands on them; you don't need to change your mind, just see from there for a moment. If you pray, you can hold that person before God.
Preferential option for the poor. In Catholic teaching, the needs of the poor come first in judging any decision, the way a sick child is served first. Today's word.
screen: `PREFERENTIAL OPTION FOR THE POOR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the poor first. The one in greatest need is served first, not loved more. Until tomorrow.

1297.title: The dignity of work
1297.hook: his hometown neighbors know Jesus by one thing: his trade
1297.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Joseph the Worker with a feast day, some dioceses offer a Labor Day Mass, and Catholic teaching on just wages and workers' associations is cited in debates about labor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lazarus at the gate, and the preferential option for the poor. Your line was the poor first.

Who was Jesus to the people who grew up with him? In Mark, he comes home to Nazareth and teaches in the synagogue, and the neighbors can't get past one thing. In the Douay-Rheims: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" The Greek word is tekton, a builder, a craftsman. Whatever the crowds had seen, his own town knew him by his trade, by hands that cut and fit and carried. Catholic teaching takes that seriously: in Christ, God worked with his hands. Today, the dignity of work.
screen: `HOME TO NAZARETH.` → `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER?` → `GOD WORKED WITH HIS HANDS.`

segments.voice: First, work isn't a punishment. In Genesis, before anything has gone wrong, the Douay-Rheims says: "the Lord God took man, and put him into the paradise of pleasure, to dress it, and to keep it." Work is there in paradise. What comes after the fall is the sweat and the thorns: work made hard, not work invented. Second, work is for the person, not the person for work. John Paul the Second wrote a whole letter on human work, and its center is this: the value of work comes first from the fact that the one doing it is a person. Scrubbing floors and running a company both carry the dignity of a human being at work. Nobody is only a cost on a spreadsheet. Third, workers have rights. Leo's Rerum Novarum told employers not to treat workers as things to make money from, and defended the right of workers to form their own associations. Later teaching names a just wage, safe conditions and rest, which the Church treats as rights, not favors. Fourth, rest belongs to work. The same Genesis that gives the garden gives the seventh day, when God rests. The Catechism calls the sabbath a protest against slavery to work and the worship of money. A day off isn't laziness in this teaching. It's a reminder that a person is more than an output.
screen: `WORK BEFORE THE FALL.` · `WORK IS FOR THE PERSON.` · `WORKERS HAVE RIGHTS.` · then, large: `REST BELONGS TO WORK.`

segments.voice: Look at one thing near you, a chair, a cup, the clothes you're wearing, and let the hands behind it come into view: someone built, grew, sewed, packed, drove, stocked, and most of them you'll never meet. Then pick one worker you will see today, a bus driver, a nurse, a mail carrier, a mechanic, and decide how you'll thank them, by name if you can, not for being nice but for the work. If you pray, you can pray for them.
The dignity of work. In Catholic teaching, work is part of how people were made, it exists for the person, and workers have rights. Today's word.
Your line: work has dignity. In this teaching, the one doing the work matters most. Rest well.

1298.title: Solidarity
1298.hook: stub a toe and the whole body stops: Paul's picture, stretched to the whole human race
1298.howItsDone: Catholics pray for people around the world in the prayers of the faithful at Mass, and some parishes support relief and development work abroad, sometimes through partnerships with a parish in another country.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the carpenter of Nazareth and the dignity of work. Your line was work has dignity.

Stub a toe on the bed frame at night, and the whole body stops. Hands reach down. The face winces. A word comes out that wouldn't be said in church. Nobody called a meeting. Paul uses that picture, writing to the Christians at Corinth about how they belong to each other. In the Douay-Rheims: "if one member suffer any thing, all the members suffer with it; or if one member glory, all the members rejoice with it." Catholic social teaching stretches that one body past the church door, to the whole human race. Today, solidarity.
screen: `A STUBBED TOE STOPS THE BODY.` → `IF ONE MEMBER SUFFER.` → `PAST THE CHURCH DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, the ground of it. In Acts, Paul stands before the council in Athens, among people whose gods are not his, and tells them, in the Douay-Rheims, that God "hath made of one, all mankind, to dwell upon the whole face of the earth." Made of one. Catholic teaching reads that as one human family, whatever the borders, languages or religions. Second, what solidarity is not. John Paul the Second wrote that it isn't a feeling of vague pity at the troubles of people far away. It's a firm, lasting commitment to the common good, to the good of all and of each, because everyone is responsible for everyone. A feeling passes when the news changes. A commitment keeps showing up. Third, how close the far-off already is. The shirt on your back was sewn somewhere; the coffee was picked by someone. Lives on opposite sides of the earth are already tied together. Solidarity asks that those ties be just, that the person at the other end of the thread is treated as family. Paul gives the daily version to the Galatians: "Bear ye one another's burdens." Fourth, it runs both ways. Look again at Paul's line. When one member suffers, all suffer; when one member is honored, all rejoice. Solidarity isn't only pity flowing downhill. It's also learning from, celebrating with, and receiving from people far away. One family shares the grief and the feast.
screen: `MADE OF ONE.` · `NOT VAGUE PITY, A COMMITMENT.` · then, large: `BEAR YE ONE ANOTHER'S BURDENS.` · then: `IT RUNS BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: Choose a place far from you, a country in the news this week, the place your clothes were sewn, a region you know almost nothing about, and let it be real people, not a map: someone waking up there, cooking, worrying about a child, laughing at something. If you pray, pray for them, as Catholics do in the prayers of the faithful at Mass; if you don't, hold them in mind as family you haven't met.
Solidarity. One human family, made of one, where one member's pain and joy belong to all, held as a firm commitment, not a passing feeling. Today's word.
Your line: one family. Cousins you haven't met yet, on the far side of every newscast. See you tomorrow.

1299.title: Care for creation
1299.hook: a saint sings to Brother Sun and Sister Water, and a pope borrows his first words
1299.howItsDone: Catholics read Pope Francis's Laudato Si' in parishes and schools, some keep a Season of Creation in the fall, and Francis of Assisi's canticle is prayed and sung around his feast day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, solidarity: one body, made of one. Your line was one family.

Brother Sun. Sister Moon. Brother Wind. Sister Water. In his Canticle of the Creatures, Francis of Assisi praises God for each of them by name, as if he were introducing his relatives. Then he calls the earth itself our sister and mother, who feeds us. Stanza after stanza, the canticle repeats the same words in the old Italian of his day: laudato si', praise be to you. When Pope Francis wrote a letter about the environment, he took its name from that refrain, and its subtitle reads: on care for our common home. Today, care for creation.
screen: `BROTHER SUN, SISTER WATER.` → `THE EARTH: SISTER AND MOTHER.` → `LAUDATO SI'.`

segments.voice: First, the goodness. Genesis looks back over everything made, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." Very good, and the verse gives no reason but that God made them. In Catholic teaching, creation has worth because God made it, not only because people need it. Second, who owns it. A psalm says, in the Douay-Rheims: "The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof." People are tenants, not landlords. The Catechism says the dominion Genesis gives humanity isn't absolute. It's a trust, and it has to respect the integrity of creation. Third, the earth and the poor together. Pope Francis wrote that damage to the environment falls hardest on the most vulnerable, and asked his readers to hear both the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor. A poisoned river is an injustice to whoever lives downstream. So care for creation isn't a separate cause beside the rest of this block; it's dignity, the poor and solidarity, all at once, with soil and water in the picture. Fourth, time. Our common home is shared across the years, not only across the globe. The Catechism names the generations to come, and Pope Francis wrote that the world people have received belongs also to those who will follow them. Somebody not yet born will drink from the same river.
screen: `VERY GOOD, BECAUSE GOD MADE IT.` · then, large: `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.` · `THE CRY OF THE EARTH AND THE POOR.` · then: `A HOME FOR THOSE NOT YET BORN.`

segments.voice: Sister Water, Francis called it: let the water you'll use today come to mind, the shower, the sink, the kettle, the dishes, the glass by your bed, and pick one place to use less, and exactly how: a shorter shower, the tap off while you brush, a full load instead of half. Then follow that water downstream in your mind, to the people and creatures who share it, now and later. If you pray, you can give thanks for it.
Care for creation. In Catholic teaching, the earth is the Lord's, very good in itself, and held in trust for the poor and for generations to come. Today's word.
Your line: our common home. Somebody downstream, and somebody not yet born, shares every river. Go gently.

1300.title: Rerum Novarum again (1891)
1300.hook: a worker signs for a wage too low to live on: is the deal fair because it was agreed?
1300.howItsDone: Catholic bishops and organizations cite Rerum Novarum in debates about minimum and living wages, and Catholic employers are urged by Church teaching to pay wages that let workers support a family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, care for creation: Brother Sun, Sister Water. Your line was our common home.

A worker needs a job, and there's no other job in sight. The owner offers a wage too small to live on, and the worker signs. Hands are shaken. Nobody was forced at gunpoint. So is that wage fair, simply because both sides agreed to it? Plenty of arguments say a deal is a deal. Leo's letter, the one this block opened with, says something else; its closing line says it was given at Rome in 1891. Today, a just wage.
screen: `NO OTHER JOB IN SIGHT.` → `IS A DEAL ALWAYS FAIR?` → `BACK TO LEO'S LETTER.`

segments.voice: First, Leo's answer. When a worker accepts harder terms because necessity, or fear of something worse, leaves no choice, he writes, the worker is the victim of force and injustice. A signature made with no real alternative doesn't make a wage just. Second, the measure. A wage, Leo says, must be enough to support a worker who lives frugally and behaves well. And he hopes for more: a wage that lets a worker support a wife and children in reasonable comfort, and still put a little aside, so that over time ordinary workers might come to own something themselves. Third, the roots in scripture. Sending out disciples in Luke, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "the labourer is worthy of his hire." The Greek word for hire there is misthos, wages. And the letter of James warns the rich that the wages held back from the workers who reaped their fields cry out, and that the cry reaches the ears of the Lord. Leo's letter stands in that line. Fourth, what it means now. The Catechism calls a just wage the legitimate fruit of work, and says that refusing or withholding it can be a grave injustice. Today people speak of a living wage, close to what Leo described. What counts as enough changes with the place and the prices. The principle stays put: in this teaching, honest work should pay enough to live on and to raise a family.
screen: `A DEAL ISN'T ENOUGH.` · `ENOUGH FOR A FAMILY.` · then, large: `WORTHY OF HIS HIRE.` · then: `THE LEGITIMATE FRUIT OF WORK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose work your day depends on: the person who stocks the shelves, the aide at a care home, the cook. Ask, without rushing to an answer, what a household in your town needs for rent, food and the basics, and whether their pay could support a family here. Just hold the question; if you pray, you can pray for them.
Just wage. In Leo's letter, a wage enough for a worker to live on and support a family, and not made just merely because it was agreed. Today's word.
Your line: a just wage. A deal alone doesn't make it fair. One thousand three hundred days now.

1301.title: Quadragesimo Anno (1931)
1301.hook: Moses is judging every case alone until his father-in-law steps in, and a pope later gives the advice a name
1301.howItsDone: Catholic teaching applies subsidiarity to families, parishes, schools and governments, and Catholics cite it in debates over which level of society should take on a task.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Leo's letter again, and a worker worthy of his hire. Your line was a just wage.

From morning until night, the people stand around Moses, waiting for him to settle their disputes. Every case, large or small, comes to one man. His father-in-law Jethro watches a day of it and tells him plainly, in Exodus, that this isn't good: he'll wear himself out, and the people with him. Choose capable, honest people, Jethro says, and set them over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. Let them judge the small matters, and bring the hard ones to you. Moses listens. Much later, a pope wrote a letter that gave Jethro's kind of advice a name. Today, Quadragesimo Anno.
screen: `ONE MAN, EVERY CASE.` → `JETHRO: THIS ISN'T GOOD.` → `SHARE THE LOAD.`

segments.voice: First, the letter. Quadragesimo anno is Latin for in the fortieth year. Pius the Eleventh opens by marking forty years since Leo's Rerum Novarum, looks back at what that letter set moving, and takes up questions it left open. Second, the principle he states, which the Church now calls subsidiarity. Pius writes that it's an injustice, and a disturbance of right order, for a larger and higher body to take over what a smaller one can do for itself. What a family can decide, the city shouldn't decide for it. What a town can handle, a national government shouldn't swallow. Third, it cuts both ways. Subsidiarity isn't simply small is good. Pius also says every social body exists to help its members, never to destroy or absorb them. So when the smaller group can't manage, when a family can't build a hospital or a village can't fight a flood alone, the larger body has a duty to step in. The Catechism puts it as support and coordination for the common good: help from above that strengthens the hands below, rather than replacing them. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary Tuesday. Subsidiarity is a form of respect. It trusts the people closest to a problem to know something about it: the manager who lets the team decide how to reach the goal, the parent who lets a teenager plan the trip, the parish that asks the food pantry volunteers before rewriting its rules. Moses wasn't weaker for sharing the load. Jethro's promise, in Exodus, was that the people would go home in peace.
screen: `IN THE FORTIETH YEAR.` · `DON'T TAKE WHAT THE SMALLER CAN DO.` · `THE LARGER EXISTS TO HELP.` · then, large: `TRUST THE PEOPLE CLOSEST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a group where you usually make the call, at work, at home, a committee or a group chat, and find one decision the people closest to it could make without you. Picture handing it over cleanly, offering help only if asked; if an urge comes to take it back, notice it and let it pass. If you pray, ask God for that kind of trust.

1302.title: Pacem in Terris (1963)
1302.hook: a pope writes on rights and peace, and addresses the letter to all people of good will
1302.tomorrow: Signs of the times (Gaudium et Spes)
1302.howItsDone: Catholics often pray for peace at Mass in the prayers of the faithful, and Pacem in Terris is still read and taught in Catholic schools, parishes and peace groups as a charter of human rights and duties.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Quadragesimo Anno: what a small group can do well, a bigger one shouldn't swallow. Your line was from the ground up.

Night, a field outside Bethlehem, and shepherds hear the sky fill with voices. In Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, the song goes: "Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will." In Latin, pacem in terris. Those words became the name of a letter from Pope John the Twenty-third. It took the angels' audience too. It's addressed to bishops, clergy and the faithful, and then, at the end of the greeting, to all men of good will. Anyone could open it and find their name on the envelope.
screen: `ON EARTH PEACE.` → `PACEM IN TERRIS.` → `TO ALL PEOPLE OF GOOD WILL.`

segments.voice: First, the list. Pacem in Terris sets out rights that belong to a person simply for being a person: life and what keeps it going, food, clothing, shelter, rest, medical care. The right to learn. To worship God as conscience directs. To work, to meet with others, to move from place to place, to take part in public life. These aren't favors a government hands out. They come with being human. Second, the other half, the pairing this block met with Cain. A right in one person brings a duty, in that same person and in everyone around them. My right to life is my duty to look after it, and your duty to respect it. A society that shouts only about rights, the letter suggests, is building with one hand. Third, what peace stands on. John the Twenty-third names four things: truth, justice, charity and freedom. Peace here isn't just the quiet after the guns stop. It's a building, and those are its four walls. Take one away, and the roof sags. A treaty table is a long way from an ordinary week. But truth told at work, a fair deal, care for a neighbor, and room for others to choose are the same four walls, built smaller. The letter takes good will as something people can practice, one wall at a time.
screen: `RIGHTS THAT COME WITH BEING HUMAN.` · `EVERY RIGHT HAS A DUTY BESIDE IT.` · `TRUTH, JUSTICE, CHARITY, FREEDOM.` · then, large: `ON EARTH PEACE TO MEN OF GOOD WILL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one table where people are trying to talk instead of fight: two countries in the news, a city council, a family that has stopped speaking. Picture them there, tired and wary, still at the table, and give each of the four walls one breath: truth, justice, charity, freedom. If you pray, hold them before God with the angels' line, on earth peace to men of good will; if you don't, keep that table in mind and wish it well.

Pacem in Terris. Peace on earth: rights, duties and four walls, for all people of good will. This week's road: the poor first, work has dignity, one family, our common home, a just wage, from the ground up, and now peace on earth. Today's word.
Your line: peace on earth. The angels sang it to anyone of good will. Until tomorrow.
